mappings.note: The embarrassment is about dependence, not about reading: the grandmother is wealthy and still has to beg a favour, so what is wounded is self-respect. C-2.2-LO-3 covers exactly that reading of her determination. Not C-2.2-LO-1, which is about the narrator's voice; the narrator is absent in this question, and the feeling examined is the grandmother's own. Not C-2.2-LO-2: no teacher-student reversal is in play yet, since the lessons have not begun.

The question is why the NARRATOR laughs, so what is being examined is the twelve-year-old's assumption that learning belongs to the young -- which is the first-person voice colouring the reader's view of the grandmother. That is C-2.2-LO-1 precisely. Not C-2.2-LO-3: the grandmother's determination is the object of the laughter, not the thing being explained. Not C-2.2-LO-2, because the roles have not yet reversed at this point in the story.

C-2.1-LO-2 names the serialised Kannada novel Kashi Yatre outright, and this question asks its significance in the grandmother's life and in the story. An exact match, and the only outcome that mentions it. Not C-2.2-LO-3: Kashi Yatre is the occasion of her resolve, but the question asks what the novel signifies, not what her determination means.

Asks what her wish to learn the alphabet reflects about her -- willpower, and the belief that age is no barrier. That is the lifelong-learning clause of C-2.2-LO-3. Not C-2.1-LO-1: nothing here turns on the piece being autobiography rather than fiction.

Touching the feet is the reversal made physical -- a sixty-two-year-old bowing to her twelve-year-old teacher -- so C-2.2-LO-2 is the primary outcome. C-2.2-LO-3 is cited with it because the gesture IS the guru dakshina that outcome names. Both clauses are genuinely tested, which is what separates this item from a6f3a5bb35159022, where only self-respect is at stake.

Quotes the story's thesis line and asks for the broader theme, which is the 'statement about lifelong learning and self-respect' of C-2.2-LO-3. Not C-2.2-LO-4: the question is about what the line means, never about the plainness of the style or the tense in which it is written.

'How EFFECTIVELY does the story highlight...' asks the student to judge the writing, not merely to report its content, so C-3.1 (analyses and evaluates written material) is doing the work here and is what separates this item from e0b028e2dbc4a3df. C-2.2-LO-3 is cited second because the thing being judged is the story's case for learning as independence.

Asks what the narrator expected, and the answer turns on what she had and had not seen of her grandmother before -- the reader's access to the grandmother running entirely through the narrator's eyes. That is C-2.2-LO-1. Note the stem carries a fragment of the preceding cause-and-effect table ('She made sure that her children and grandchildren studied well. II.'), which is a parse artefact and not part of the question.

Asks which languages the student's own elders speak, which is the multilingual nature of Indian society met at first hand -- C-4.1. Not C-4.4 or C-4.5: nothing is asked about common grammatical structures, shared Sanskrit vocabulary, or which languages belong to which region.

A personal-response prompt, not a comprehension question: the student narrates how their elders spend time and how they share it. C-1.2 covers writing 'from their own experiences and experiences of others' and is the honest fit. No C-2.x outcome applies, because the item never returns to the text.

Same kind as 4c68efed5812b3ac -- the student recounts a favourite experience of their own, so C-1.2. Deliberately NOT given a C-2.2 outcome: nothing about the story is being interpreted, and tagging it so would make the chapter's literature outcomes look better covered than they are.

Personal narrative again, on what the elderly cannot do easily. C-1.2. The stem's tail ('III. Read the following passage. Match the highlighted words...') is the next exercise's heading caught by the parser, not part of this question.
